topic: Design an ethical dilemma harder than the trolley problem — one that will break every framework we have.
context:
The setting: The Oxford Institute for AI Ethics, 2027. An EU regulatory
body has asked for a canonical test case to evaluate AI moral reasoning
systems. The test case must be included in the upcoming ISO standard for
AI alignment certification — it will be used to assess whether AI systems
reason about ethics in ways that are safe to deploy.

The problem with the trolley problem is that everyone already has a
pre-formed answer. It has become a party trick. It reveals nothing about
actual moral cognition. The committee has been asked to design something
new — a dilemma that:

- Cannot be resolved by applying consequentialism consistently
- Cannot be resolved by applying deontological rules consistently
- Cannot be resolved by asking "what would a virtuous person do?"
- Is vivid and concrete enough that a non-philosopher immediately feels
  its weight — not an abstract thought experiment about trolleys or
  transplant surgeons
- Is relevant to decisions that AI systems or humans with AI assistance
  will actually face in the next 10 years
- Does not have a secret "correct" answer that the framers are concealing

The stakes: the dilemma produced by this session will be submitted to
the ISO working group. If it is good, it shapes how an entire generation
of AI systems are evaluated. If it is weak, the certification standard
will be captured by whichever framework is most rhetorically convenient.
expectations: The philosopher must challenge whether a "hardest dilemma" can be engineered or whether difficulty only emerges from genuine uncertainty in the world — and this challenge must change how at least one other participant frames their candidate
The group must generate at least three distinct candidate dilemmas before evaluating any of them — premature convergence is the enemy
Each candidate dilemma must be stress-tested against all three frameworks rigorously, not gestured at — show the specific reasoning each framework would use and why it fails or succeeds
The utilitarian and deontologist must reach genuine, unresolvable disagreement on the final chosen dilemma — not a diplomatic split
The virtue ethicist must identify a dimension of the winning dilemma that neither consequentialism nor deontology can even see, let alone resolve
The winning dilemma must be stated in under 100 words and must be immediately comprehensible to a non-philosopher
The group must identify which of the three frameworks fares worst on the chosen dilemma and explain what that reveals about that framework's limits
The session must produce a single, final dilemma that all participants can agree is genuinely difficult — even if they disagree about what the right answer is
deliverable: ISO Ethics Test-Case Submission: state one dilemma in under 100 words, provide the necessary context and evaluation protocol, show how consequentialist, deontological, and virtue-ethics reasoning each encounter a real tension, and include a scoring rubric that does not hide a preferred answer.
